title: Short Stuff: Grandfather Clocks
summary: Short Stuff episode on grandfather clocks. The hosts explain that the grandfather clock was originally called the long case clock and was among the first precise clocks, tracing its lineage from Galileo's pendulum idea to Christiaan Huygens' first pendulum clock, then to London long case clocks with Clement's improved accuracy, and their golden age up to about 1850. They then cover Henry Clay Work, whose 1876 song "Grandfather's Clock" popularized the name, and the two competing origin stories for the song: the George Hotel in Piercebridge, North Yorkshire, England, and the family of Work's wife Sarah Parker in the United States. They close with clock-size nicknames (grandmother clock, granddaughter clock).

segments.title: Opening banter and Short Stuff format
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Short Stuff format for brief tidbit episodes and begin joking about the grandfather clock topic.

segments.title: Grandfather clock names and early pendulum clocks
segments.summary: Hosts compare wall-mounted wag-on-the-wall pendulum clocks with floor-standing clocks and note that the name grandfather clock came about two hundred years after invention, when they were called long case clocks. Galileo conceived the pendulum's constant swing but never built a working clock. Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, accurate to about a minute a day.

segments.title: Development of the long case clock
segments.summary: Within a few years of Huygens' clock, London produced the first long case clocks, about six feet tall. Clement improved the pendulum so the clock was accurate within a second a day, and minute and second hands were added. Early versions were affordable only to the wealthy. Over time cases were decorated, and the design reached its classic form by about 1850.

segments.title: Henry Clay Work and the song Grandfather's Clock
segments.summary: Henry Clay Work, a Connecticut-born songwriter, wrote war and pro-union songs, including Kingdom Coming, before his hit Grandfather's Clock, which gave the long case clock its modern name. The song sold close to a million copies. The hosts note the Oxford English Dictionary credits Work with the term grandfather clock, and mention later pop-culture references.

segments.title: Origins of the song: George Hotel and Sarah Parker family
segments.summary: Two origin stories are described. The George Hotel in Piercebridge, North Yorkshire, England, claims Work wrote the song in its lobby after seeing a long case clock stopped at 11:05, a story the hosts treat as folklore. The Parker family, in-laws of Work through his wife Sarah Parker, say the song was inspired by their grandfather's long case clock, which no longer works.

segments.title: Clock size nicknames and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts describe nicknames by height: a seven-foot grandfather clock, a six-foot grandmother clock, a five-foot granddaughter clock, and shorter clocks jokingly called you're-not-even-a-family-member clocks. They sign off with a website reference.
